## Virtualized

The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, section headings included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its selection and highlight kept. A pinned heading sits over the list without moving any row, so where each row lies is unchanged by it.
Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. Its scroll position is clamped to its ends before a frame is drawn, never drawn past an end and corrected the frame after, and kept in whole device pixels, so a row never shimmers between two places. What lies at an end stays at it: a running row's time ticking, a task finishing, a row added or removed elsewhere in the list, or the tab being resized never makes the rows in view jump and settle. A list scrolled to its bottom stays at its bottom as rows are added, and one at its top stays at its top. The list counts as taller than the tab only once it overflows it by a whole pixel, as the right sidebar's panels do, so a list that fits never scrolls at all.
Scrolled to its bottom, the last row shows whole, its bottom edge at the bottom of the tab's visible area, never cut off by even a pixel, and nothing lies beneath it but the list's own bottom padding of 8 pixels. The list's height is the sum of its rows, headings and day dividers included, and that padding, measured in the same device pixels the rows are drawn at, and its scrollable height is that less the height of the area it is drawn in: the right sidebar's own visible area, never an area that counts a sticky heading, the open task's back bar, or the scrollbar's own room as part of the list. Headings pinned at the bottom take room from the list's visible area, as those at the top do, so scrolled to the bottom, the last row still shows whole above any heading pinned there, and none ever hides a row. However the tab is resized, by the window, the sidebar's panels, or the sidebar's width, the bottom is worked out anew in that frame, so a list scrolled to its bottom still shows its last row whole.

## Days

Within Previous, tasks are grouped by the day they were sent, in the user's local time, each day headed by a divider row, 28 pixels tall like every row, its label in small muted text set in to line up with the rows' text: "Today", "Yesterday", the weekday for the rest of the past week, as "Tuesday", and the date beyond that, as "3 October", with the year added once it isn't this one, as "28 September 2025", then, muted after it, how many tasks that day holds. Days run oldest to newest, as the tasks do, and only days with a task are shown; a chain is under the day its first step was sent. While filters are on, a day with no task shown is left out, and its count is of the tasks shown. The labels follow the clock: one reading "Today" reads "Yesterday" once midnight has passed, without reopening the tab.
A day's divider is sticky beneath Previous's own heading: while its tasks are scrolled through, it stays pinned just below that heading, until the next day's divider pushes it out, so the day of the rows in view always shows. Day dividers take the place of the session dividers the previous tasks had; a session that starts a new conversation shows a small muted mark at its first row's right instead, its tooltip saying it started a new conversation.

content.text:
The Tasks tab now keeps its list of rows instead of rebuilding it every frame, and the new test passes. A running task's tick no longer works the rows out again.

**The spec doesn't say this yet.** The compiled `TasksTab.virtualized` doesn't have the new rule, and its reference file is older than this chain. The "spec step" output pasted into this prompt is my previous reply, not the spec step's. I went ahead under the cost rule `TasksTab.virtualized` already states ("cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten"). The rule asked for still needs adding to the spec.

**What changed** (in `src/prompt_mode/tasks_tab.rs`):
- **Kept rows:** a new `Timeline` holds the rows, where the headings, day dividers and queued rows lie, and an index from each row's key to its place. Previous's task count is in it too, so the heading no longer recounts.
- **When it's rebuilt:** whenever `PromptMode` changes, which covers tasks added or changing status, filters, and sections opening or closing. It's also rebuilt at midnight, and when the number of tasks or queued prompts changes. Ticks, spinners, streaming and scrolling never rebuild it.
- **Each rebuild is cheaper:**
  - The chain layout is worked out once, not three or more times.
  - Previous and Running mark the tasks held in chains in a flag list, so finding them is no longer square in the task count.
- **No searching per frame:** the top row is found from the key index. The pinned day divider and the next divider or heading are found by binary search over where they lie.
- **Test:** `the_tasks_tab_keeps_its_rows_while_a_task_runs` opens the tab with 10,000 previous tasks and one running. After the sidebar settles, three seconds of ticks neither rebuild the rows nor redraw the Tasks tab. Scrolling halfway down redraws the tab from the rows it kept.

**Tests:** I ran them in a scratch copy with empty stand-ins for the prompt files the sandbox blocks. The new test and the related Tasks tab, redraw and slide tests pass. The `main_window`, `prompt_mode`, `scrollbar` and `project_tree` suites have 21 failures. None is new. Twenty need `piton` or `git`, which the sandbox blocks. The other is `scrollbar::tests::the_bar_is_the_column_on_its_side`, which only uses its own test views and was failing before this change.

**A caveat:** rebuilding on any `PromptMode` change is broader than the rule you described. Something unrelated, like opening a file tab, also rebuilds the rows once. That's still never per frame, and never on a tick.
